analogy.p: Imagine a water pipe with a gate that opens wider as more sunshine falls on it. In the dark the gate is almost shut, so very little water (current) flows; in bright light the gate swings open and water flows freely. The wider the gate, the lower the resistance to the flow. The analogy breaks down because the LDR responds only to light and the thermistor only to heat, and the real reason is that more electrons are freed to carry charge, not that a gate moves.
analogy.t: A tap that opens wider in the sunshine (or when it is warm)

bullets: An **LDR** is a resistor whose resistance depends on **light intensity**.
A **thermistor** (the type on the AQA specification is the **negative temperature coefficient** type) is a resistor whose resistance depends on **temperature**.
Both are **non-ohmic** components: their resistance is **not constant**, so a graph of current against p.d. is not a straight line through the origin for all conditions.
Both are used as **sensors** in automatic control systems, where a changing resistance causes a changing current or p.d.
Resistance is still worked out with **resistance = potential difference / current**, whatever component it is.
Light intensity is how much light energy hits a surface each second; temperature is a measure of how hot the surroundings are.
You must always state **both** the quantity that changes (light intensity or temperature) **and** the direction of the resistance change.
core.h: What LDRs and thermistors are and why they matter
core.p: A **light-dependent resistor (LDR)** and a **thermistor** are both **sensors**: components whose **resistance changes automatically in response to the surroundings**. An LDR responds to **light intensity** and a thermistor responds to **temperature**. Because their resistance changes, the current through them and the p.d. across them also change, and this electrical signal can be used to switch other devices on or off. That is why they appear in night lights, thermostats and fire alarms. The AQA specification wants you to state how each one behaves, draw and recognise their circuit symbols, and use them in circuits.

bullets: Bright light: **low resistance**, large current for a given p.d.
Dim light or darkness: **very high resistance**, tiny current.
Graph shape: a **decreasing curve** from the top-left to the bottom-right, never reaching zero.
The change is **automatic and reversible**: move the LDR back into the dark and its resistance rises again.
Typical uses: **automatic night lights**, **street lights** that come on at dusk, **light meters** in cameras, and **burglar alarms** triggered by a change in light.
In a question, say 'as light intensity increases, the resistance of the LDR decreases' using these exact words.
An LDR does not respond to temperature in a way you need to know at GCSE; keep the two sensors separate.
core.p: The resistance of an LDR **decreases as light intensity increases**. In bright light its resistance is low, so charge flows through it easily; in the dark its resistance is very high, so very little current flows. This is an **inverse relationship in direction**: more light means less resistance. The graph of resistance against light intensity is a **curve that falls steeply at first and then flattens out**, not a straight line, so the resistance is not inversely proportional in a precise mathematical sense that you need to calculate at GCSE.

bullets: Hot: **low resistance**, larger current.
Cold: **high resistance**, smaller current.
Graph shape: a **curve that falls steeply at low temperature and flattens at high temperature**.
The effect is **automatic and reversible**.
Typical uses: **thermostats** for central heating, **fire alarms**, **digital thermometers**, **car engine temperature sensors**, **electric ovens**, and **incubators**.
Learn the word pair: **temperature up, resistance down**.
A thermistor responds to the temperature of its surroundings or of whatever it touches, so it must be placed where it will sense the temperature you care about.
core.p: The resistance of a **thermistor decreases as the temperature increases**. At low temperature the resistance is high and the current is small; when the thermistor is warmed, its resistance falls and the current for the same p.d. becomes larger. The graph of resistance against temperature is again a **decreasing curve**. The AQA specification is only concerned with this type, called an **NTC (negative temperature coefficient) thermistor**, so unless a question tells you otherwise always give this behaviour.

bullets: More light energy or heat energy releases more **free electrons**, so more **charge carriers**.
More charge carriers means a **larger current** for the same p.d.
Using R = V / I, a larger I with the same V means a **smaller R**.
In a **metal conductor** the opposite happens: higher temperature gives **greater resistance** (more ion vibration).
The thermistor and LDR therefore behave in the opposite way to a heated filament lamp.
This is a good example of the idea that resistance depends on the material **and** on the conditions.
If asked to explain, always link: energy supplied, more carriers, bigger current, smaller resistance.
core.h: Why does the resistance fall? (explaining the reason)
core.p: Both devices are made from **semiconductor** materials. In a semiconductor at low temperature or in the dark, most of the electrons are tightly held in the atoms, so only a few **charge carriers** are free to move and the resistance is high. When the thermistor is heated, or light shines on the LDR, **more electrons gain enough energy to break free** and become charge carriers. With more charge carriers able to move, a **larger current flows for the same p.d.**, so the resistance (V divided by I) is lower. This is different from a metal wire, where heating makes the resistance go up because the ions vibrate more and collide with the moving electrons more often. You are not usually asked to explain the semiconductor effect in detail, but knowing it helps you remember the direction.

bullets: **Fixed resistor**: rectangle with a wire at each end.
**LDR**: rectangle within a circle, with two arrows pointing at the circle.
**Thermistor**: rectangle with a diagonal line through it.
**Variable resistor**: rectangle with an arrow through it (a different component, do not confuse it with the thermistor).
**Ammeter** is a circle with A and goes **in series**; **voltmeter** is a circle with V and goes **in parallel** across the component.
**Cell** is a long thin line and a short thick line; the long line is the positive terminal.
Marks are lost for drawing the arrows pointing away from the LDR or for drawing gaps in the circuit.
core.p: Exam papers show these components with standard symbols, and you must be able to recognise and draw them. A **fixed resistor** is a plain rectangle. The **LDR** is a rectangle inside a circle with **two arrows pointing inwards** towards the circle, representing light falling on it. The **thermistor** is a rectangle with a **diagonal line through it** that bends at the bottom end into a short horizontal hook. When you draw a circuit, use a ruler, keep corners square and make sure every component is in a complete loop.

bullets: Always read the correct axis: resistance is usually on the vertical (y) axis.
Describe the trend with direction and data, e.g. 'resistance falls from 800 ohms at 10 degrees C to 200 ohms at 50 degrees C'.
Say the rate of change is **greatest at low values** and slows as the curve flattens.
To read a value, draw a vertical line from the x value to the curve, then horizontally to the y axis, and take a careful reading.
Use the units: **ohms (symbol Omega)** for resistance, **degrees C** for temperature.
Do not extend a curve beyond the data unless asked; extrapolating a curve is unreliable.
Check scale divisions carefully, since the grid squares are often not worth one unit each.
core.p: Questions often give a graph or table of resistance against light intensity or temperature and ask you to read values, describe the trend or use R = V / I. When you describe a trend, state the **overall pattern**, quote data to support it, and mention if the rate of change slows down. Both graphs are curves that fall quickly and then level off. Because the line is curved, you must read values using the curve itself, not by assuming a straight-line pattern.

bullets: Independent variable: **light intensity** (changed by distance from lamp) or **temperature** (changed by heating the water).
Dependent variable: **resistance**, calculated from p.d. and current.
Control variables: the **same cell p.d.**, the same component, and other light sources kept constant (use a dim room or a screen).
For the thermistor, make sure the thermistor is **waterproofed** and stir the water so the temperature is even.
Switch off between readings so the component does not heat itself.
Plot resistance against light intensity or temperature and draw a **smooth curve** of best fit.
Repeat readings and take a mean to improve reliability.
core.p: You can investigate an LDR or thermistor by measuring its current and p.d. at different conditions and calculating resistance. Connect the component in **series with a cell (or power supply), an ammeter and a switch**, and put a **voltmeter in parallel** across the component. For the LDR, change the light intensity by moving a lamp to different measured distances; for the thermistor, put it in a beaker of water and heat the water, measuring temperature with a thermometer. At each setting record V and I, then calculate **R = V / I**.

bullets: Total resistance in series = **R1 + R2** (add the resistances).
Current is the same everywhere: **I = V total / R total**.
The p.d. across each component: **V = I x R**.
Total p.d. = sum of the p.d.s across each component, so a drop across one means a rise across the other.
**Dark LDR**: high resistance, large share of p.d. across the LDR.
**Bright LDR**: low resistance, small share of p.d. across the LDR, so more p.d. across the fixed resistor.
Swapping the positions of the fixed resistor and sensor reverses which way the output p.d. changes.
core.h: Using a sensor with a fixed resistor (series circuit)
core.p: In a **series circuit the same current flows through every component, and the cell p.d. is shared between the components in proportion to their resistances**. The component with the **larger resistance takes the larger share of the p.d.** If an LDR is in series with a fixed resistor, then in the dark the LDR has the high resistance, so it takes most of the p.d.; in bright light its resistance falls, so its share of the p.d. falls and the fixed resistor's share rises. By measuring (or using) the p.d. across the sensor, a circuit can detect light or temperature. This is the idea behind the sensing circuit in the figure.

bullets: **Night light**: dark, LDR resistance high, p.d. across LDR high, lamp turns on.
**Street light**: same principle, on at dusk, off at dawn.
**Thermostat**: cold, thermistor resistance high, heating turns on; warm, resistance low, heating turns off.
**Fire alarm**: high temperature, thermistor resistance low, current large, alarm sounds.
**Greenhouse or incubator** temperature control uses thermistors with heaters.
The device that actually switches on the lamp or heater (such as a relay or transistor) is beyond the GCSE specification; you only need to explain the change in resistance, current or p.d.
In an answer, always give the chain: condition changes, resistance changes, current or p.d. changes, device responds.
core.p: A sensor on its own does not switch anything; it changes the current or p.d., and another part of the circuit responds to that change. In a simple **automatic night light**, the LDR's resistance rises in the dark, which changes the p.d. across a switching component and turns the lamp on; in daylight the LDR's resistance falls and the lamp turns off. A **thermostat** works in the same way with a thermistor: when the room cools, the thermistor's resistance rises and the heating is switched on, and when the room warms up its resistance falls and the heating is switched off. A **fire alarm** uses a thermistor that falls in resistance as the temperature rises, so the greater current can trigger the alarm.

bullets: **Fixed resistor**: constant resistance, straight line I-V graph through the origin.
**Filament lamp**: resistance increases with temperature, I-V curve flattens.
**Diode**: very high resistance in the reverse direction, low in the forward direction.
**Thermistor**: resistance **decreases** with temperature, the opposite trend to the filament lamp.
**LDR**: resistance decreases with light intensity.
If a component's resistance changes, its I-V graph is **not a straight line**.
Gradient on an I-V graph is not simply the resistance for a curve; use R = V / I at each point.
core.p: It helps to compare the LDR and thermistor with the other components in the I-V topic. A **fixed resistor at constant temperature** is ohmic: current is directly proportional to p.d., giving a straight line through the origin. A **filament lamp** has a curved I-V graph because its resistance **increases** as the filament gets hot. A **diode** only allows current in one direction. An LDR and thermistor are different again because their resistance changes due to **external conditions** (light or surrounding temperature), not just the current through them.

bullets: R = V / I (unit: ohm), V = I x R (unit: volt), I = V / R (unit: ampere).
Convert **mA to A** by dividing by 1000; convert kilo-ohms to ohms by multiplying by 1000.
Series: **R total = R1 + R2**.
Check: p.d. across LDR + p.d. across fixed resistor = cell p.d.
Give the answer with a unit and to a suitable number of significant figures.
Show each step, since marks are given for working even if the answer is wrong.
Use the graph or table to find the sensor's resistance in the given conditions first.
core.p: Calculations use the same relationships as all circuits. **Resistance (ohms) = potential difference (volts) / current (amperes)**, rearranged as **V = I x R** and **I = V / R**. For a sensor in series with a fixed resistor, first find the **total resistance** by adding, then the **current** using the cell p.d., then the **p.d. across each component**. Always convert milliamperes to amperes (divide by 1000) before substituting, and check that your final answer is sensible: the p.d.s across the components must add up to the cell p.d.

bullets: Link to **series and parallel circuits**: sharing of p.d. and the same current in series.
Link to **I-V characteristics**: non-ohmic behaviour of lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors.
Link to **energy transfers**: a heater controlled by a thermistor transfers energy to the thermal store.
Link to **power**: P = I x V, so a larger current from a smaller resistance gives more power.
Link to **safety**: large currents heat wires, so circuits include fuses.
Link to **sensing in everyday technology**: fridges, ovens, phones that dim the screen.
Link to **required practicals**: control variables, repeats, and graph skills.
core.p: This topic connects to several others. Current, p.d. and resistance underpin all of **4.2 Electricity**. The idea of charge carriers links to **current as the rate of flow of charge**. The thermistor's response links to **energy transfer by heating** because the temperature depends on the energy transferred. The control of heating in houses links to **energy efficiency and insulation** and the topic on **domestic electricity** and fuses. The required practicals on resistance and I-V characteristics use similar circuits.

bullets: **1 mark**: state the direction, e.g. 'resistance decreases'.
**2 marks**: direction **plus** the cause, e.g. 'as light intensity increases, resistance decreases'.
**3 marks**: add the effect on current or p.d.
**4 and 6 marks**: structured chain of reasoning in the correct order.
For circuit diagram questions, include a **complete loop** and correct symbols.
If asked for a use, link the sensor to its job: 'a thermistor in a thermostat detects the temperature'.
Do not write 'the LDR gets hot' or 'the thermistor reacts to light'; mixing the sensors loses marks.
core.p: Typical questions on this topic are short. 'State' or 'Give' needs a single fact, such as the effect of increasing temperature on a thermistor. 'Describe' needs the pattern with direction, and 'Explain' needs the chain of reasoning, linking the change in conditions to the change in resistance, current and p.d. For higher-mark questions you may be asked to design a simple circuit, so be ready to name the components, say how they are connected and describe the result. Always keep your language precise: use the words 'resistance', 'current' and 'potential difference' correctly.

exam: 1 mark (state): give the direction of change only, e.g. 'resistance decreases' - but always name the condition too.
2 marks (describe): direction plus cause: 'as temperature increases, the resistance of the thermistor decreases'.
3 marks: add the effect on current or p.d. in the circuit, e.g. 'so the current increases'.
4 marks (explain): chain of reasoning - condition changes, resistance changes, current or p.d. changes, device responds.
6 marks (extended): plan or explain a complete system, such as a thermostat; use correct order, correct terms and a conclusion.
Command words: **state/give** = one fact; **describe** = what happens; **explain** = why; **evaluate** = weigh up.
For calculations, write the equation (R = V / I), substitute with units, then give the answer with a unit.
Always convert mA to A (divide by 1000) before using the equation.
Graph tips: label axes with quantity and unit, plot accurately, draw a smooth curve (not dot-to-dot), and read from the curve.
Circuit diagrams: use a ruler, correct symbols, a complete loop, ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel.
Check units carefully: ohms for resistance, volts for p.d., amperes for current.
Use the exact phrases 'light intensity' and 'temperature'; avoid vague words like 'brightness' or 'heat' on their own.

mistakes.r: The resistance of an LDR decreases as the light intensity increases.
mistakes.w: The resistance of an LDR increases as light gets brighter.

mistakes.r: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as temperature increases (it behaves opposite to a metal wire or filament).
mistakes.w: A thermistor's resistance increases as it gets hotter, just like a wire.

mistakes.r: An LDR responds to light intensity; a thermistor responds to temperature. Do not mix them.
mistakes.w: The LDR gets brighter / reacts to heat.

mistakes.r: Resistance changes because more charge carriers are freed; the current increases as a result, not as the cause.
mistakes.w: The resistance falls because the current increases.

mistakes.r: Both graphs are curves that fall quickly then level off.
mistakes.w: The graph is a straight line.

mistakes.r: A variable resistor is adjusted by hand; a thermistor changes automatically with temperature.
mistakes.w: The thermistor is the same as a variable resistor.

mistakes.r: Resistance is measured in ohms; current is in amperes.
The arrows point towards the LDR because light falls on it.
mistakes.w: In the LDR symbol the arrows point away because it gives out light.

mistakes.r: A voltmeter must be connected in parallel across the component; the ammeter is in series.
mistakes.w: Voltmeter in series with the sensor.

summary: You need to know that the resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR) decreases as light intensity increases and that the resistance of a thermistor decreases as temperature increases, and be able to use them in circuits. This matters because these sensors turn changes in the environment into changes in current and potential difference, which is how everyday control systems like thermostats and night lights work.

worked.ans: 500 ohms at 20 degrees C and 150 ohms at 60 degrees C: the resistance decreased by 350 ohms as the temperature increased, as expected for a thermistor.
worked.q: A thermistor is connected in series with a cell and an ammeter. At 20 degrees C the p.d. across the thermistor is 4.0 V and the current is 8.0 mA. At 60 degrees C the p.d. across it is 3.0 V and the current is 20 mA. Calculate the resistance of the thermistor at each temperature and state the change. (4 marks)
steps: Convert current to amperes: 8.0 mA = 0.0080 A; 20 mA = 0.020 A.

worked.ans: The p.d. across the LDR is 6.75 V in the dark and 3.0 V in bright light, so it falls as light intensity increases because the LDR's resistance falls and it takes a smaller share of the 9.0 V.
worked.q: An LDR is in series with a 2000 ohm fixed resistor and a 9.0 V cell. In the dark the LDR has resistance 6000 ohms; in bright light it has resistance 1000 ohms. Calculate the p.d. across the LDR in each case. (5 marks)
steps: p.d. across LDR = I x R = 0.001125 x 6000 = 6.75 V.
Check: in the dark, the fixed resistor has 9.0 - 6.75 = 2.25 V.

worked.ans: As the room cools, the resistance of the thermistor increases, so the p.d. across it increases and the current falls. This change is detected by the switching part of the circuit, which switches the heater on. When the room warms up, the thermistor's resistance decreases, the p.d. across it falls and the heater is switched off, so the temperature stays roughly constant.
worked.q: Explain how a thermistor can be used to switch a heater on when a room gets cold. (4 marks)
steps: State the sensor behaviour: thermistor resistance is high when cold.
Link to circuit: a high resistance means the p.d. across the thermistor rises (and current falls).
Link to device: this change in p.d. or current triggers the switching circuit that turns the heater on.
